title: Hecke selection concretely couples Euler factors to modular functional symmetry
claim: The abstract two-sided L-function package has a concrete modular realization: simultaneous Hecke eigenvectors make Fourier coefficients multiplicative and hence produce Euler factors, while the Mellin completion transports modular transformation symmetry into a functional equation. The two analytic features are therefore outputs of two compatible structures on the same eigenform, not unrelated axioms.
historical_or_program_relation: This construction-level account sharpens the program in which zeta is treated as a prototype and the wider L-function class is studied to expose the arithmetic or geometric source of its analytic package.
limits: Hecke diagonalization applies to the stated modular setting; it neither gives a modular origin for classical zeta nor proves that every axiomatically admissible L-function is automorphic. An Euler product plus functional equation does not force critical-line zeros.

title: Analytic self-duality can be manufactured, while geometric pairing sign cannot
claim: For a nonreal Dirichlet character, multiplying the completed L-functions of χ and its conjugate makes the reflection internal to one analytic object without changing the union of their zeros. By contrast, orthogonal or symplectic type is a pairing sign transported through motivic, ℓ-adic, and automorphic realizations and can obstruct criticality at the center. Thus self-functional-equation form and representation-theoretic self-duality carry different information.
historical_or_program_relation: The Dirichlet-family extension shows how GRH survives dual pairing, while the later motivic program refines the word self-dual into a sign invariant with arithmetic consequences.
limits: The product L(s,χ)L(s,χ̄) changes degree and does not turn either factor into a geometric object. The pairing-sign argument uses the stated regularity and algebraicity assumptions and a conjectural motivic bridge; neither construction proves GRH or transfers a conclusion to ζ.

title: Persistent rank, root-number parity, and bulk symmetry are separate channels
claim: Low-zero behavior in an L-function family must be decomposed before assigning a symmetry type: persistent central zeros are removed as a rank contribution, root numbers split symplectic families into parity subfamilies, and a parity-sensitive off-diagonal prime–Kloosterman term distinguishes SO(even) from SO(odd) even when the diagonal does not.
historical_or_program_relation: This refines random-matrix family classification from a single bulk label into independent arithmetic mechanisms for central mass, functional-equation sign, and the first symmetry-sensitive density correction.
limits: These are family-level low-zero statistics, not statements about every member or about classical ζ. The cited off-diagonal calculation uses its own support range and GRH input for Dirichlet L-functions; rank, root-number balance, and bulk type cannot be inferred from one another.

title: Trace-formula diagonalization may change the family measure
claim: Petersson weighting is what turns a cusp-form average of Hecke coefficients into a diagonal plus a controlled Kloosterman–Bessel off-diagonal, but the same weighting defines a different probability measure from unweighted counting. When the weight is itself a fluctuating central L-value, weighted low-zero density can display a symmetry signature inconsistent with the representation-theoretic type of the unweighted family.
historical_or_program_relation: A standard analytic access mechanism becomes an estimand audit: the trace formula supplies the family average, and later symmetry work identifies removal of its natural weights as an additional proof obligation.
limits: This does not invalidate the exact weighted Petersson identities or show that every harmonic weight changes symmetry. The two cited families and weight normalizations are not identical; an unweighted conclusion requires a separate weight-removal argument.

title: A zero-mass local condition removes the trace formula's main counting signal
claim: Trace-formula family statistics depend on a main term carried by the identity orbit: in positive-volume harmonic families it becomes Plancherel mass, analogous to the Petersson diagonal that normalizes Hecke averages. Imposing a Plancherel-null local condition deletes that leading mass, so ordinary limit-multiplicity machinery cannot isolate the desired subfamily before any zero-symmetry test begins.
historical_or_program_relation: The mechanism marks a boundary in the automorphic-family program: increasingly arithmetic or cohomological local restrictions may make the natural trace tool lose its counting baseline.
limits: Petersson's GL(2) formula and the general Arthur-trace setting are examples of the same signal/error architecture, not the same theorem. Failure of the main term does not imply that the constrained family is empty or that its symmetry conjecture is false; it identifies a method bottleneck.

title: Geometric and classical trace formulas linearize different objects
claim: In the finite-field model, intersecting a graph with the diagonal becomes an alternating cohomological trace because the diagonal is the identity kernel. Classical explicit formulas instead use ζ'/ζ, contour residues, and Fourier test functions to turn prime powers and zeros into dual distributions; Lefschetz-style kernel restriction explains why a fixed-point formula has trace coefficients but does not identify the classical arithmetic distribution with a Frobenius trace.
historical_or_program_relation: The classical prime–zero formula motivated trace interpretations, while algebraic geometry supplies an exact graph–diagonal mechanism against which proposed spectral analogues can be tested.
limits: The finite-field equality has an actual variety, map, and Weil cohomology; the classical formula is an analytic distributional identity. No graph, cohomology group, or Frobenius operator for ζ follows from their formal resemblance, and a trace identity alone supplies no positivity or RH.

title: Correspondences become a zero-location mechanism only after a positive adjoint is supplied
claim: The historical move from elliptic endomorphisms to higher-genus self-correspondences constructed the algebraic carrier but left the norm or positive-definite form missing. Weil forms later isolate the needed positive-adjoint interface on algebraic correspondences, and the finite-field index theorem turns the corresponding sign into zero-location control; the classical explicit-formula criterion likewise exposes a uniform sign as the unfilled burden.
historical_or_program_relation: The sequence separates discovery of the right operators from discovery of the form that constrains their spectrum, explaining why correspondence algebra alone did not complete the positive-characteristic proof program.
limits: Weil-form positivity, surface-intersection negativity, and the classical test-function quadratic form are related proof roles, not identified forms. Their domains and sign conventions differ, and the finite-field mechanism does not provide the missing classical correspondence or prove ζ-RH.

title: Finite-field functional symmetry acts on a finite Frobenius spectrum
claim: Both curve zeta functions and classical completed zeta expose reciprocal zero symmetry, but only the finite-field setting compresses all extension-field point counts into a rational generating function with finitely many Frobenius inverse roots. There the functional equation pairs reciprocal roots and upgrades a one-sided radius bound to exact modulus q^(1/2); classical completion makes the involution visible without supplying a finite point-count spectrum.
historical_or_program_relation: The solved function-field analogue clarifies which extra representation—not merely the shared functional equation—makes its RH accessible.
limits: q^(1/2)-modulus is a function-field weight statement, not the classical line Re(s)=1/2 under a literal change of variables. Classical ζ has no source-supported Frobenius action or finite rational numerator here, so the finite-field proof cannot be transferred by analogy alone.

title: Period-polynomial circle roots concern an encoding of critical modular L-values
claim: For a Hecke eigenform, a period integral packages finitely many critical L-values as coefficients of a reciprocal polynomial. In the large-weight proof, a zero-transparent exponential model supplies monotone boundary phase and a separate uniform error bound transfers its sign changes to unit-circle roots. This is a finite coefficient-encoding theorem whose symmetry ultimately comes from the modular functional equation.
historical_or_program_relation: The construction is a genuine modular descendant of the L-function package, but it relocates the zero problem from the analytic L-function to an auxiliary polynomial where phase and perturbation estimates are available.
limits: The circle zeros are zeros of the period polynomial, not zeros of L(f,s), and they imply neither GRH for the modular L-function nor RH for classical ζ. The argument needs its stated weight/level regime and error inequality; reciprocal symmetry alone does not force circle roots.

title: A polynomial critical-line analogue is proved by finite recurrence geometry
claim: A symmetry-preserving integral transform sends x↦1−x invariance to a polynomial functional equation s↦1−s, so recentering makes its critical-line claim a real-rootedness problem just as completion and s=1/2+it do for ξ. The proof then uses a finite recurrence, continuity in a parameter, interlacing, and exclusion of common-root collisions through a cubic characteristic equation.
historical_or_program_relation: The example isolates how reflection symmetry can be combined with an independent finite-dimensional root-control mechanism, offering an analogue of the formulation rather than a route to the classical conjecture.
limits: These transformed polynomials have finite degree and a recurrence/interlacing structure absent from the cited classical ξ formulation. Their functional equation has no demonstrated Euler product, prime explicit formula, or ζ-divisor content; their real-rootedness does not imply classical RH.

title: Dirichlet-polynomial proofs succeed by matching witnesses to mean-value inputs
claim: The zero-density argument first reflects an overlong expression through the functional equation into a dual finite sum plus remainder, then combines correlation control with fourth moments; powering a zero-detecting polynomial moves its witness into the admissible length regime of that large-value theorem. A mollifier uses a complementary design—approximate inversion and an exact low-range coefficient gap—to place L-times-mollifier inside an averaged norm estimate.
historical_or_program_relation: Across Dirichlet L-function methods, finite polynomials are engineered interfaces between zeros or near-inversion and the scale at which family mean values are actually controllable.
limits: Powering a zero detector and multiplying by a mollifier are not interchangeable: one transfers zero witnesses to density bounds, the other suppresses coefficients on average. Neither proves a zero-free half-plane or GRH, and the OCR-damaged zero-density span does not support exact lengths, exponents, or thresholds beyond the qualitative assembly.

title: Family formation trades individual control for deformable statistical leverage
claim: Placing L-functions in a conductor- or parameter-varying family changes the target from locating every zero of one function to estimating a population observable. In quadratic families this lets large-sieve or density tools prove nonvanishing and rank information, or rule out the scenario that every sufficiently large member has an exceptional real zero, without resolving each member separately.
historical_or_program_relation: This is a deliberate weakening that turns otherwise inaccessible individual questions into average theorems while preserving central-point and low-zero information that high-zero universality can forget.
limits: There is no formal universal notion of family in the number-field setting, and conclusions depend on the chosen parametrization, conductor ordering, and measure. Positive proportions or average rank bounds do not prove GRH for any unspecified member and say nothing directly about classical ζ.

title: Two statistical abstractions preserve symmetry while discarding different arithmetic data
claim: Automorphic trace formulas push local Plancherel measure through an L-map to obtain Satake-parameter statistics, retaining a local representation-theoretic origin for Euler factors. Characteristic-polynomial models instead retain symmetry type and conductor-scaled zero density to predict universal moment structure, while leaving the prime-local Euler product to a separate arithmetic factor.
historical_or_program_relation: The comparison gives a staged family program: derive local parameter laws from spectral counting, then test which aggregate zero or value statistics depend only on symmetry and which still remember Euler arithmetic.
limits: A Plancherel pushforward is not a derivation of random-matrix moment conjectures, and the matrix model does not reconstruct Satake parameters or Euler factors. The cited moment comparisons concern primitive families and provide conjectural or numerical calibration, not individual RH or a classification of ζ.

title: Prime–zero trace encoding does not itself force zero location
claim: The explicit formula is an exact trace-like bridge: test functions turn the logarithmic derivative into dual prime-power and zero distributions. Its usefulness for RH begins only when an additional sign or spectral constraint forces location; family positivity is presently operational, while random-matrix spacing and finite-field cohomology identify plausible structural obligations but do not supply the missing classical operator or index theorem.
historical_or_program_relation: The trace and random-matrix programs refine the classical explicit formula from an encoding into a search for the extra positivity, self-adjointness, or geometry that would make the encoding restrictive.
limits: Matching spectral statistics is not construction of a Hilbert–Pólya operator, and a proposed spectral representation is not useful solely because its trace resembles the explicit formula. Finite-field geometry is an analogue, family positivity gives separate average results, and none of these observations proves ζ-RH.

title: Coefficient positivity lets a global boundary constrain every local Euler root
claim: In both finite-field and automorphic settings, a positive-coefficient auxiliary Dirichlet series prevents cancellation at its convergence boundary. Landau's theorem can then turn the location of a global singularity into one-sided bounds on local Euler-factor roots; Rankin–Selberg constructions make that positivity structural by converting local power sums into nonnegative quadratic coefficients.
historical_or_program_relation: The shared mechanism shows how global analytic continuation can control local spectra only after passing to a positivity-preserving auxiliary L-function, complementing geometric weight arguments.
limits: The auxiliary series, convergence boundary, and local parameters differ between the two settings. Landau positivity yields one-sided local bounds under its hypotheses, not critical-line zero location, purity by itself, or RH for classical ζ.
